question: How do I hire a fractional CRO for a healthtech business?
body:
## Direct Answer

To hire a fractional CRO for a healthtech business, define the specific revenue problem you need solved (pipeline, GTM motion, payer contracting, or a raise), then source operators who have carried a quota inside regulated healthcare — not just generic SaaS — and hire them on a fixed weekly-hours retainer with 90-day outcome milestones. Prioritize domain fluency in HIPAA-bound sales cycles, provider and payer buying committees, and clinical-evidence-driven procurement, because a healthtech deal is not a horizontal B2B deal wearing a lab coat.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior commercial leader who works part-time — usually one to three days a week — across a defined engagement rather than as a full-time executive. For a healthtech company, the appeal is obvious: you get someone who has already built a payer-provider sales motion, without paying a full C-suite salary and equity package before you have the revenue to justify it. But the healthtech context changes the hiring calculus in ways that generic "how to hire a fractional CRO" advice misses entirely. Below is the operator's playbook for finding, vetting, structuring, and getting value from a fractional CRO in a regulated healthcare market.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a healthtech company?

A fractional CRO owns the commercial engine — the connective tissue between marketing, sales, customer success, and often partnerships — and is accountable for the number, not just for activity. In an early or growth-stage healthtech business, that usually means one of three concrete mandates: building a repeatable go-to-market motion from a founder-led sales base, fixing a stalled pipeline where deals die in procurement or security review, or preparing the commercial story and metrics for a raise or acquisition. The healthtech twist is that "the number" is entangled with reimbursement models, evidence requirements, and multi-stakeholder buying committees that a horizontal SaaS CRO has never navigated.

Concretely, expect a strong fractional CRO to diagnose your revenue architecture in the first 30 days, then operate and coach for the remainder of the engagement. They will rebuild your ICP around actual healthcare buyers (a hospital VP of clinical operations behaves nothing like a mid-market IT director), redesign the sales stages to reflect real healthcare deal gates like security assessments and clinical champion sign-off, and install forecasting discipline your board can trust. The difference between a fractional CRO and a fractional VP of Sales matters here: the CRO holds the whole revenue system, including retention and expansion, which in healthtech is where the real margin lives once you survive the brutal land motion. For the deeper distinction, see our breakdown at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11412](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11412).

It helps to be precise about what a fractional CRO is *not*, because the title is misused constantly. They are not a super-SDR who will personally cold-call your way to a pipeline; if you need someone dialing all day, you need reps, not an executive. They are not a strategy consultant who leaves a deck; the whole point is that they operate inside your deal reviews and pipeline every week. And they are not a fundraising advisor who happens to know sales — although a good one can materially strengthen a raise, that is a byproduct of building a credible commercial engine, not the core job. In healthtech specifically, the fractional CRO often becomes the internal translator between the clinical, regulatory, and product functions and the commercial reality of the market, because founders in this space are frequently clinicians or researchers who have never run a quota-carrying team. That translation work — turning clinical conviction into a buyable, evidence-backed, reimbursement-aware value proposition — is one of the most underrated things a seasoned healthtech revenue leader delivers, and it rarely shows up on a job description.

## How do I know if my healthtech business is actually ready for a fractional CRO?

Readiness is the single most common mistake founders make. Hiring a fractional CRO too early — before you have any repeatable signal of demand — turns an expensive operator into a very expensive SDR. The role is a force multiplier on an existing motion, not a substitute for product-market fit. A useful readiness test: do you have at least a handful of closed deals that a founder sold, some understanding of who your economic buyer is, and a product a stranger can be sold on? If a founder has never closed a deal and you cannot articulate why the last three prospects said no, you have a product or positioning problem that a CRO cannot paper over.

The second readiness dimension is specific to healthtech: regulatory and reimbursement clarity. If your revenue model depends on a reimbursement pathway you have not validated, or your data handling has not cleared a real HIPAA and security review, a CRO will spend the engagement blocked by things outside the commercial function. Get those foundations at least legible before you bring in a revenue leader, or scope the CRO's mandate to explicitly include untangling them. The diagram below maps the readiness decision an operator should walk through before signing anyone.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Considering a fractional CRO] --> B{Founder has closed real deals}
    B -->|No| C[Fix product market fit first]
    B -->|Yes| D{Reimbursement and HIPAA path is legible}
    D -->|No| E[Scope CRO to untangle foundations or wait]
    D -->|Yes| F{Clear revenue problem to solve}
    F -->|No| G[Define the mandate before hiring]
    F -->|Yes| H[Ready to hire a fractional CRO]
```

Notice that every path that skips a gate leads to wasted spend rather than to the hire. The readiness work is not a formality — it is what makes the engagement produce a return. Founders who rush past it tend to churn through two or three fractional leaders before realizing the problem was upstream. For a fuller readiness framework across revenue roles, see [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11256](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11256).

There is also a cash and runway dimension to readiness that founders under-weight. A fractional CRO is a real monthly expense, and the healthcare sales cycle is long — pilots, security reviews, and committee approvals routinely stretch six to eighteen months before revenue lands. That means you should hire a fractional CRO only when you have enough runway for the motion they build to actually mature; bringing one on with three months of cash left, hoping they will conjure bookings before the wall, almost always ends in a rushed, discount-heavy scramble that damages your pricing and your reputation with early health-system buyers. Map the CRO's expected impact against your runway honestly. If the math only works when deals close faster than healthcare deals ever close, you are not ready — you are hoping. The most disciplined founders write down, before they hire, exactly which leading indicators (qualified pipeline, stage conversion, champion depth) they expect to move within the runway they have, and treat those as the real test of whether the engagement is working, rather than waiting on slow-closing bookings to tell them something they could have seen months earlier.

## Where do I find qualified fractional CROs with real healthtech experience?

The supply of people who call themselves fractional CROs has exploded, and most of them have zero regulated-healthcare experience. Your sourcing strategy has to filter hard for domain fluency. The highest-signal channels are warm: ask other healthtech founders, your investors, and your board who they have actually worked with and would hire again. Healthcare-focused venture firms and accelerators often keep informal benches of fractional operators they trust, because they have watched these people perform across their portfolio. A referral from someone who has seen the operator carry a healthtech number is worth more than any polished LinkedIn profile.

Beyond warm intros, look at fractional-executive marketplaces and networks, healthtech-specific communities and Slack groups, and the alumni of companies that sold successfully into your exact buyer. Someone who ran regional sales at an established EHR vendor, a payer-facing analytics company, or a digital-health platform that reached scale has muscle memory you cannot teach in an engagement. Be skeptical of the generalist "fractional CRO" who has done a dozen horizontal SaaS gigs and lists healthcare as one logo among many — the healthcare sales cycle punishes tourists. When you evaluate a candidate's background, weight relevant scars over relevant titles.

Pay particular attention to *which corner* of healthcare an operator actually sold into, because the domain is not monolithic. Selling clinical software into hospital systems is a different sport from selling to payers, which is different again from selling to physician practices, life-sciences companies, employers, or direct-to-consumer digital health. A CRO who spent a decade closing enterprise deals with integrated delivery networks may have thin instincts for a self-serve, PLG-flavored motion aimed at independent clinics, and vice versa. When you build your sourcing list, tag each candidate by the buyer type they have genuinely carried a quota against, and prioritize the ones whose lived experience matches your specific go-to-market. The closer their prior buyer is to your buyer, the less of your runway they spend learning your market on your dime.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Sourcing channels] --> B[Investor and board referrals]
    A --> C[Healthtech founder network]
    A --> D[Fractional exec marketplaces]
    A --> E[Alumni of proven health vendors]
    B --> F[Shortlist of 4 to 6]
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G[Structured vetting on domain fit]
    G --> H[Hire on 90 day milestones]
```

The goal of sourcing is a shortlist of four to six real candidates, not a single obvious pick. A small competitive process surfaces how each operator thinks about your specific problem and gives you leverage on scope and terms. For how to run that vetting conversation, keep reading.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire an expensive generalist?

Vetting a fractional CRO is fundamentally about testing for pattern-matching against your reality. The single best interview technique is a live teardown: give the candidate a real, anonymized snapshot of your pipeline or a stalled deal and ask them to diagnose it in the room. A genuine healthtech operator will immediately ask about the buying committee, the security review status, the clinical champion, the reimbursement model, and where in the stage progression deals are actually dying. A generalist will talk about MEDDIC and cadences in the abstract. The specificity of their questions is the signal.

Reference checks matter more than usual because fractional operators leave a trail of short engagements, and short engagements can hide a pattern of leaving before results land. Talk to at least two founders who worked with the candidate, and ask the un-flattering question directly: what did they fail to deliver, and would you hire them again? Probe for whether they operated or merely advised — many "fractional CROs" produce a strategy deck and disappear, when what you need is someone who will sit in deal reviews and coach your reps every week. Finally, verify domain-specific competence with pointed questions: how have they handled a hospital security assessment stalling a deal, how do they think about pilot-to-contract conversion, and how do they build a champion inside a health system. Vague answers here are disqualifying. Our reference-check and interview scorecard framework lives at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11298](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11298).

One more vetting dimension is cultural and structural fit with a fractional model. The best fractional CRO for you is one whose availability, communication rhythm, and willingness to be measured on outcomes match how your team actually works. Ask how many other engagements they carry, how they handle a deal emergency on a day they are not scheduled with you, and how they prefer to be held accountable. An operator who bristles at defined milestones is telling you something.

Consider running a short, paid trial before committing to a full engagement — a two- to four-week diagnostic sprint in which the candidate audits your pipeline, interviews a few reps and customers, and returns a written revenue-architecture assessment with a 90-day plan. A paid trial does three things at once: it lets you see the operator's actual work product rather than their interview polish, it surfaces how they interact with your team under real conditions, and it gives you a low-cost exit if the fit is wrong. Strong operators generally welcome this structure because it also lets *them* qualify *you* — whether your data is legible, whether the founder will actually cede commercial authority, and whether the problem is one they can move. Be wary of any candidate who insists on a long, locked-in retainer with no trial and no early off-ramp; confidence is good, but refusing to be evaluated on real work is a flag, not a feature. Watch, too, for the operator whose references are all glowing but suspiciously vague on outcomes — press every reference for a specific number that moved, and be honest with yourself when the answer is a story instead of a metric.

## How should I structure the engagement, scope, and compensation?

Structure the engagement around outcomes and defined time, not around a vague "advisor" relationship. The two common models are a fixed monthly retainer for a set number of days or hours per week, and a hybrid of a smaller retainer plus performance-linked upside tied to pipeline or bookings. For most healthtech companies, a clear weekly-hours retainer with explicit 30-60-90 day deliverables produces the least ambiguity: a diagnostic and revenue-architecture recommendation by day 30, an installed and operating motion by day 60, and measurable pipeline or forecasting improvement by day 90. Write these milestones into the agreement so both sides know what success looks like before money changes hands.

On compensation, avoid inventing a number from thin air — the right figure depends on the operator's seniority, the days per week, and your stage, and it is best discovered through your competitive shortlist rather than a fixed rule. What matters more than the headline rate is aligning incentives without distorting behavior: pure commission on a long healthcare sales cycle can push a fractional leader toward short-term discounting or over-promising, so most healthtech engagements weight the retainer and use modest, milestone-based upside. Always include a clear term (a 90-day initial engagement with a renewal decision is common), a defined scope so the CRO is not quietly absorbed into unrelated founder tasks, and clean IP and confidentiality terms given the sensitivity of healthcare data. The trade-offs to hold in mind are outcome clarity, incentive alignment, and the operator's genuine availability — a beautifully structured deal with someone who is over-committed across five other clients will still underperform a simpler deal with someone who has the bandwidth to sit in your pipeline every week.

Two contractual details deserve extra care in a regulated-health context. First, data and compliance terms are not boilerplate here: a fractional CRO will touch pipeline data, and possibly customer contact information tied to health-system relationships, so make sure your agreement addresses confidentiality, any Business Associate Agreement obligations if they could encounter protected health information, and clean assignment of any IP or process they build for you. Second, be explicit about conflicts of interest — a fractional operator carrying several engagements should not be quietly advising a direct competitor, and your agreement should name that boundary rather than assume it. These clauses are cheap to add up front and expensive to litigate later, and a seasoned healthtech operator will expect them without being asked.

The final structural decision is the exit or transition plan. A fractional CRO is, ideally, a bridge — they build the motion, hit the milestones, and either transition to a lighter advisory cadence or hand off to a full-time hire they helped you recruit. Bake that transition into the engagement from day one so the relationship has a natural arc rather than becoming an indefinite retainer that quietly loses accountability. The healthiest fractional engagements know from the start how they are meant to end.

## What does the first 90 days actually look like with a fractional CRO?

Because so much of the value of a fractional CRO is concentrated in a short, high-leverage window, it is worth walking through what a well-run first 90 days looks like in practice, so you can hold your operator to it. In the first 30 days the work is almost entirely diagnostic: the CRO interviews the founder, the reps, a handful of won and lost customers, and often a friendly buyer or two inside a target health system, then maps your real funnel against your claimed funnel. The deliverable is not a motivational deck; it is an honest revenue-architecture assessment that names where deals actually die — usually in security review, committee alignment, or a missing clinical champion rather than in the top-of-funnel activity founders tend to obsess over.

In days 30 through 60, the operator moves from diagnosis to installation. That means rebuilding your pipeline stages to reflect true healthcare deal gates, rewriting qualification criteria around the economic buyer and the reimbursement story, standing up a forecast the board can actually trust, and coaching reps live in deal reviews rather than lecturing them in a training. By days 60 through 90 you should see leading indicators move — cleaner qualified pipeline, better stage-to-stage conversion, tighter forecasts, and often a couple of stalled deals unstuck — even if bookings themselves lag because healthcare closes slowly. If, at the 90-day mark, all you have is activity and optimism with no movement in the leading indicators you agreed on up front, that is your signal to have a hard conversation rather than to auto-renew. The whole point of the milestone structure is to make that conversation objective instead of emotional. For how selling into health systems shapes those deal gates in the first place, see [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11377](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11377).

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant advises and produces recommendations; a fractional CRO operates — they own the number, sit in deal reviews, coach reps, and are accountable for revenue outcomes on defined milestones, not just for a strategy document.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run three to twelve months. A common shape is a 90-day initial engagement with renewal decisions, extended until the motion is repeatable and either handed to a full-time CRO or reduced to a light advisory cadence.

### Can a fractional CRO help us raise our next round?
Yes — a strong one builds the commercial metrics, forecast credibility, and GTM narrative investors scrutinize, and can join diligence calls. Confirm fundraising support is explicitly in scope, since not every revenue operator has raise experience.

### Should a seed-stage healthtech startup hire a fractional CRO or a full-time VP of Sales?
If you lack a repeatable motion, a fractional CRO to architect it is usually the better first move. Hire a full-time VP once the motion is proven and you need day-to-day execution scale.

### Do fractional CROs work on commission?
Some do, but pure commission is rare and risky on long healthcare cycles. Most work on a retainer, occasionally with modest milestone- or pipeline-linked upside to keep incentives aligned without encouraging short-term discounting.

## FAQ

**How much does a fractional CRO cost?**
Cost varies with seniority, days per week, and your stage, so discover the right figure through a competitive shortlist rather than a fixed benchmark. The structure matters more than the headline rate: most healthtech engagements use a weekly-hours retainer with modest milestone-based upside, always well below a full-time C-suite salary plus equity load.

**How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?**
Typically one to three days per week, defined explicitly in the agreement. Fewer than one day rarely allows real operating involvement; more than three starts to approach full-time cost without full-time commitment.

**What healthtech-specific experience should I require?**
Look for someone who has carried a quota selling into providers, payers, or health systems — navigating HIPAA and security reviews, clinical champions, multi-stakeholder buying committees, pilot-to-contract conversion, and reimbursement-linked value propositions. Horizontal SaaS experience alone is insufficient for a regulated healthcare motion.

**Can one fractional CRO cover multiple companies at once?**
Yes, that is the model — most carry two to four engagements simultaneously. Ask directly how many they hold and how they handle an urgent deal on a day they are not scheduled with you, so you understand their real availability.

**What should the first 90 days deliver?**
A common milestone set: a revenue diagnostic and go-to-market architecture by day 30, an installed and operating motion with rebuilt pipeline stages by day 60, and measurable improvement in pipeline health or forecast reliability by day 90. Write these into the agreement.

**How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
Track leading indicators (qualified pipeline created, stage conversion, sales-cycle length, forecast accuracy) alongside bookings, since healthcare deals close slowly. Agree on the specific metrics before the engagement starts so you are not renegotiating success criteria mid-stream.

**What are the biggest risks of hiring a fractional CRO?**
The main risks are hiring a generalist with no regulated-healthcare fluency, hiring before you have product-market fit, an under-defined scope that lets the role drift, and no transition plan so the retainer runs indefinitely without accountability. Each is preventable with disciplined vetting and a milestone-based agreement.

**Should the fractional CRO help hire my permanent team?**
Ideally, yes. A good fractional CRO helps define and recruit the reps, sales leaders, or eventual full-time CRO who will inherit the motion, and can help onboard them. Make team-building and succession an explicit part of the scope if that is your goal.

**Do I need a Business Associate Agreement with a fractional CRO?**
If the operator could access protected health information in the course of the work, then yes — treat them like any other vendor who touches PHI and put the appropriate confidentiality and BAA terms in place. Even when they only touch pipeline data, clean confidentiality and IP-assignment clauses are worth adding up front.
